newsitem.title: USA: CIA said to have evidence Iran gave Bosnia leader cash.
newsitem.headline: CIA said to have evidence Iran gave Bosnia leader cash.

text.p: The CIA has evidence that Iranian agents secrety delivered at least $500,000 in cash to Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic for his campaign before elections there, The Los Angeles Times reported on Tuesday.

Citing classified Central Intelligence Agency documents, the newspaper reported that the agency discovered the Iranians gave Izetbegovic at least two pieces of luggage stuffed with money, each containing about $250,000, to help fund his campaign in the weeks leading up to the vote.

CIA analysts believe that Izetbegovic has been "co-opted by the Iranians" and is now "literally on their payroll", according to a classfied report based on the CIA's analysis of the issue, the Los Angeles Times reported.

The newspaper report said Clinton administration officials acknowledged on Monday that President Bill Clinton agreed to release $100 million worth of U.S. military aid to Bosnia even after the CIA uncovered the Iranian payments to Izetbegovic and reported the information to policymakers.
The aid had been withheld from the Bosnians for months because of U.S. concerns about continuing Iranian influence in the country.

The CIA declined comment Tuesday on whether it had evidence that Iran secretly sent at least $500,000 in cash to Izetbegovic. But it said its analysis supported Clinton's decision to certify that the Bosnian government was complying with its undertakings at the 1995 Dayton, Ohio, peace talks that ended 3 1/2 years of civil war.

"The (CIA) analysis indicates that Iranian arms shipments have stopped and that military and intelligence links have been broken as required by those (Dayton) undertakings," CIA spokesman David Christian said.
At the State Department, spokesman John Dinger also refused to comment directly on "allegedly leaked documents about alleged intelligence reports."
But he said while Bosnia clearly still has cultural, diplomatic and economic ties with Iran, the department is satisfied military and intelligence cooperation between Sarajevo and Tehran has ceased.
"President Izetbegovic has clearly favoured Bosnia's security orientation toward the West," Dinger told reporters.

He referred to Izetbegovic's decision, under U.S. pressure, to insist that all organised units of Iranian fighters leave Bosnia after the 1995 peace deal was signed and to fire two defence officials with close Iranian ties.
"We are confident that he at the very least respects our concerns over Iranian influence and we are satisfied that he is taking our concerns seriously," Dinger said.
But Dinger said the United States remained watchful of possible improper Iranian influence in Bosnia and had created a joint commission with the Bosnian government to investigate any such claims.

Yossef Bodansky, director of the House of Representatives Task Force on Terrorism and Unconventional Warfare, said he had no doubt that Iran had sent more than $500,000 to Izetbegovitch and his closest confidants in recent years based on what he called reports from Iranian and Bosnian informants.

In addition, Bodansky, who was among the first to raise questions about the scope of Iran's influence in Bosnia, said "thousands" of Iranian Mujahideen and Revolutionary Guards had integrated themselves into the Bosnian military and intelligence services.
"We are just looking the other way," he said in a telephone interview. "Their (Iran's) influence is growing rather than diminishing."
